description.p: baz is a music player for people who own their music. Point it at a folder and your albums are the home screen: click one and it plays front to back, gapless. There is no account, no subscription and no network service between you and your files.

It is built around claims that can be checked rather than advertised. Gapless continuity is asserted sample-for-sample in the test suite; the output device follows the sample rate of the music instead of resampling it silently, and says so on screen when a device leaves it no choice.

ul.li: FLAC, WAV, MP3, M4A/MP4 (AAC and ALAC) and Ogg Vorbis
Gapless album playback, with the per-format trim measured and tested
Multichannel files folded to stereo by the ITU-R BS.775 matrix
Albums grouped by album artist, with lossless and lossy copies kept as separate editions of one album
Incremental library scanning that re-reads only what changed on disk, across as many folders as you name
Search across the whole library as you type, by song and by record
Playlists kept as ordinary .m3u8 files you can edit anywhere else
ReplayGain, both the tags other scanners wrote and a full EBU R128 pass of your own library
MPRIS2, so desktop media controls, the lock screen, playerctl and hardware media keys all drive it

description.p: This is a public beta. The core loop is finished and nothing baz does loses or corrupts anything — it reads your files and never writes to them — but it is pre-1.0 and it has rough edges. The ones we know about, including the formats it cannot play, are listed on the project page rather than left to be discovered.

description.p: Baz is easier to install: releases now include a Linux Flatpak bundle, a Windows installer and a macOS disk image, alongside the archives for people who prefer them.
A new ten-band equaliser is available from every page. It can be fully bypassed, shows the curve it is applying, keeps boosted music from clipping with automatic headroom, and saves your own presets.
This release also adds AIFF and Ogg Vorbis, an oscilloscope and a chromeless Now Playing view, fuller keyboard navigation, and safer handling for missing playlist entries and untagged compilations.

Smart playlists are built around the line now. Draw how the music should move from the first song to the last — ten points to pull about — and the songs appear beside it. Your words are an optional filter rather than the main event, because a drawn line is something you can check by ear and a description is a guess.

Baz also says what it heard: the quietest, loudest, slowest and fastest records in your collection by name, the tempo range in beats per minute, and which of the five things it listens for your music barely varies in. Claims you can check in a second, rather than a summary you have to take on trust.
Searching for “and” now finds “&”, right-clicking in a playlist no longer sends it back to the top, and Now playing fits what is in it.
Repeat now repeats the list as well as the track. The playlist page groups A–Z like the library does, and a new playlist starts from a tile on it rather than a button.

Vibe playlists are drawn: a line over your own collection says how energetic the music should be as the playlist goes on, and after composing you can see exactly where every chosen track landed against it. Tempo, brightness, dynamics and texture can each be drawn as lines of their own. Everything is still analysed on this device, and your audio never leaves it.

The first release. baz scans a folder of music, shows the albums as the home screen, and plays them front to back with the gaps between tracks measured away. FLAC, WAV, MP3, M4A and Ogg Vorbis; search as you type; playlists; and MPRIS2 for the desktop's own media keys.
A public beta. It reads your files and never writes to them.
